title: Remove One Cell, See What Fails

scenes.tts: Delete a gene in the whole animal, and you learn what a protein does, not what a cell type does. A deletion from birth is a developmental experiment: the animal can adjust before you test it. Remove chosen cells instead; ask whether they are needed.
scenes.visual: A big field of cells in three shapes; a gene deleted in every cell from birth, a timeline where the animal adjusts; then the green cell type is removed (dashed ghosts) and a test box shows a question mark.
scenes.narration: Delete a gene in the whole animal, and you learn what a protein does, not what a cell type does. A deletion from birth is a developmental experiment: the animal can adjust before you test it. Remove chosen cells instead; ask whether they are needed.

scenes.tts: Before gene-targeted toxins, a laser could kill one identified cell. A young larva is held still with azide. Most worm cells sit in reproducible positions, and each type has a typical nucleus under Nomarski optics, so position plus nucleus names the cell. The beam is focused on a single spot, aligned with that cell. Pulses are brief, so heat has little time to spread to neighbours. In one nineteen ninety-five system, they lasted three nanoseconds. An hour to a day later, the killed nucleus is gone.

scenes.tts: A laser needs a see-through animal. A genetic toxin reaches any cell that carries its receptor, even deep in the brain. Mouse cells are poor targets for diphtheria toxin; the human receptor binds it with about a hundred thousand times higher affinity. So the human receptor gene goes under a chosen gene's control, or into an allele where Cre removes a stop cassette blocking the receptor, so a Cre line chooses the cells.
scenes.visual: Laser stops at opaque tissue while orange toxin reaches a deep cell with a purple receptor; then a construct strip where Cre removes a STOP before the receptor gene and only the Cre cells carry receptors.
scenes.narration: A laser needs a see-through animal. A genetic toxin reaches any cell that carries its receptor, even deep in the brain. Mouse cells are poor targets for diphtheria toxin; the human receptor binds it with about a hundred thousand times higher affinity. So the human receptor gene goes under a chosen gene's control, or into an allele where Cre removes a stop cassette blocking the receptor, so a Cre line chooses the cells.

scenes.tts: The toxin is injected when you choose. For example, a hundred micrograms per kilogram, on two days, seventy-two hours apart. Inside a sensitive cell, it inhibits protein synthesis. Because the timing is yours, the same cells can be removed in a newborn or an adult.
scenes.visual: A syringe injects toxin into an animal block; receptor cells die; a protein-synthesis bar falls in one cell; a timeline shows the same removal at newborn or adult.

scenes.tts: Results have two parts: a count of target cells left, and a behaviour compared with controls. In one study, over ninety-eight percent of M R G P R D neurons were gone. The mechanical withdrawal threshold rose from zero point four one grams to zero point nine nine, with no significant change in wild-type littermates given the toxin. Heat and cold sensitivity were not reduced.
scenes.caption: Results have two parts: a count of target cells left, and a behaviour compared with controls. In one study, over 98% of Mrgprd neurons were gone. The mechanical withdrawal threshold rose from 0.41 grams to 0.99, with no significant change in wild-type littermates given the toxin. Heat and cold sensitivity were not reduced.
scenes.visual: Three panels: cells left (under 2 percent), threshold 0.41 to 0.99 g with wild-type no significant change, heat and cold not reduced.

scenes.tts: The toxin might act on animals without the receptor, so give it to wild-type littermates. Too few cells might die, so count them. One Cre-driven toxin killed Paneth cells incompletely; a receptor knock-in removed virtually all. In one mouse line, the toxin depleted two spleen macrophage types. Check other cells, and use a second method.
scenes.visual: Three columns: wild-type controls given toxin, counting survivors (Cre-driven vs knock-in), bystander cells dying and a second method.

scenes.tts: In nineteen eighty-one, Kimble and White used a laser to kill a worm gonad's distal tip cell. Germ cells that would divide entered meiosis instead. In nineteen eighty-seven, Austin and Kimble found that G L P one mutants mimic this, which led to a Notch-like receptor. The laser was needed because no gene was yet known.
scenes.caption: In 1981, Kimble and White used a laser to kill a worm gonad's distal tip cell. Germ cells that would divide entered meiosis instead. In 1987, Austin and Kimble found that glp-1 mutants mimic this, which led to a Notch-like receptor. The laser was needed because no gene was yet known.
scenes.visual: A gonad tube with a distal tip cell at one end; laser kills it and germ cells switch from dividing to meiosis; glp-1 mutant mimics it, arrow to Notch receptor.

scenes.tts: In two thousand five, Luquet and colleagues killed A G R P neurons in adult mice, causing rapid starvation. Killed in newborns, the same neurons had minimal effect on feeding. Timing exposed compensation. In twenty nineteen, van Es and colleagues removed Paneth cells, yet L G R five stem cells persisted. Keep this rule: removal shows whether cells are needed, for that assay, age and targeting tool, not what they can do alone.
scenes.caption: In 2005, Luquet and colleagues killed AgRP neurons in adult mice, causing rapid starvation. Killed in newborns, the same neurons had minimal effect on feeding. Keep this rule: removal shows whether cells are needed, for that assay, age and targeting tool, not what they can do alone.
